strengths: Addresses a timely and crucial research problem: evaluating hybrid mobile GUI agents that combine low-level UI interactions with programmatic shortcuts (APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts), which has been largely overlooked by existing pure-GUI benchmarks.

Comprehensive experimental setup and baselines: evaluates a wide variety of agent frameworks, including agentic workflows (T3A, MobileAgentV2, M3A), general-purpose vision-language models (Qwen-VL series, GLM-4.5V), and specialized GUI foundation models (UI-TARS, ScaleCUA, MAI-UI).

Dual-perspective evaluation: uniquely assesses not only the agent's ability to select and execute predefined shortcuts under noisy conditions, but also tests the agent's capacity to synthesize, generalize, and reuse newly generated shortcuts from execution history.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: incorporates 9 informative metrics (notably MSRS normalized against human pure-GUI baselines) and validates the automated two-stage LLM judge against 278 human-annotated trajectories, demonstrating strong alignment (F1 > 95%).
Clear insights on shortcut selection, failure modes, and the brittleness of coordinate-based macro replay versus dynamic semantic shortcuts.
weaknesses: The dataset size (139 tasks across 11 applications) is relatively modest compared to some static GUI datasets, although understandable given the dynamic emulator-based execution and environment setup costs.

Shortcut retrieval is simplified in practice: the agent uses an application-scoped keyword filter rather than realistic open-domain or embedding-based retrieval from a large, uncurated repository, which eases the decision complexity for the agents.
The project page URL is left blank in the abstract and introduction, making it unclear whether code and environment snapshot configurations will be fully open-sourced for external verification.

Limited exploration of agent fallback mechanisms: the benchmark would benefit from evaluating how gracefully agents recover and switch back to manual GUI navigation when a shortcut call returns an unexpected error or runtime exception.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely paradigm shift in mobile GUI agents by systematically combining flexible GUI actions with efficient programmatic shortcuts (APIs, deep links, RPA scripts).
Presents a comprehensive evaluation setup featuring 139 realistic single-app and cross-app tasks across 11 popular Android applications, supported by a knowledge base of 88 curated shortcuts.

Conducts extensive baseline evaluations across diverse agentic workflows, open-source/closed-source general-purpose MLLMs (Qwen3-VL series, GLM-4.5V, Gemini), and specialized GUI models (UI-TARS, GUI-Owl, ScaleCUA, MAI-UI).

Provides valuable empirical insights into shortcut misuse, showing that shortcut augmentation is not strictly monotonic with scale and can harm performance when base models suffer from low shortcut selection precision.

Proposes a standardized framework to evaluate agent-generated shortcuts (replay vs. coordinate-free dynamic shortcuts) and thoroughly validates the automated evaluation pipeline against 278 human-annotated trajectories with high agreement (F1 > 95%).
weaknesses: The benchmark size is relatively modest (139 tasks across 11 applications) compared to recent large-scale mobile benchmarks (e.g., LlamaTouch or SPA-Bench), which somewhat limits task diversity.
The shortcut retrieval mechanism relies on simple keyword-based app matching, which largely bypasses the challenge of real-world tool retrieval and selection in large, open-domain tool spaces.

The exploration of agent-generated shortcuts reveals severe fragility in existing methods (e.g., 10% SSR for task-level replays), functioning primarily as a diagnostic testbed rather than proposing effective solutions to make generated shortcuts robust.

Evaluation on live third-party commercial applications (Amazon, YouTube, Booking.com) introduces inherent reproducibility and maintenance challenges over time due to backend API deprecation and server-side UI A/B testing.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in mobile agent research by formalizing and benchmarking hybrid GUI-shortcut execution (combining visual/UI actions with programmatic APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts) rather than relying exclusively on step-by-step GUI interactions.

Comprehensive benchmark design and metrics: includes 139 multi-step single- and cross-app tasks across 11 real-world applications, measuring not only task success rates but also execution steps (MSRS relative to human baselines), runtime, token consumption, and shortcut precision/recall.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation spanning diverse agent paradigms (workflow-based such as MobileAgentV2 and T3A vs. Agent-as-a-Model) and model families (Qwen-VL series, GLM-4.5V, and specialized GUI models like UI-TARS, ScaleCUA, and MAI-UI).

Novel evaluation framework for shortcut generation from agent execution trajectories, providing valuable empirical insights into the fragility of static macro replays versus dynamic coordinate-free shortcuts.
Thorough validation of the automated two-stage evaluation protocol (MAS-Bench-Eval) against 278 human-annotated trajectories, demonstrating strong alignment (F1 > 95%).
weaknesses: The overall benchmark size is somewhat modest (139 tasks and 88 predefined shortcuts across 11 apps), which may limit the statistical diversity of task distributions and shortcut interaction patterns.

The shortcut retrieval mechanism relies on keyword-based application filtering, which shields agents from realistic large-scale tool retrieval challenges where hundreds of candidate shortcuts across dozens of apps must be ranked and retrieved.

The shortcut generation experiments are conducted on a 50% task subset and restricted to T3A as the base executor, leaving open how well these generation strategies transfer to vision-centric models or different prompting paradigms.
Maintenance and reproducibility in live, dynamic app environments remain a long-term challenge as third-party services, UI layouts, and network-dependent app functionalities evolve over time.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in mobile device automation by formalizing a hybrid paradigm that combines low-level GUI navigation with high-level programmatic shortcuts (APIs, deep links, RPA scripts).

Provides a multi-faceted evaluation protocol measuring not only task success rates, but also execution time, step ratios relative to optimal human paths, token consumption, and shortcut invocation accuracy.

Investigates both predefined shortcuts and agent-generated shortcuts (macro replay and dynamic grounding), offering valuable empirical insights into why current LLM agents struggle to synthesize robust automation workflows from experience.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across different agent paradigms (screenshot-based MobileAgent vs. UI hierarchy-based T3A) and LLM capacities (Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.0-Flash), supported by a detailed taxonomy of failure modes.
weaknesses: The benchmark scale is relatively modest, comprising 139 tasks across 11 applications, and only 69 tasks for the shortcut generation experiments, which may limit statistical power and comprehensive coverage of rare UI states.

Evaluations rely on live, dynamic Android applications (e.g., Amazon, Booking.com, YouTube) running inside an emulator, which makes long-term reproducibility difficult due to frequent external UI redesigns, regional app variations, and potential account/network flakiness.

The mechanism for automated task verification is adapted from SPA-Bench but lacks a formal human-agreement study or quantitative verification of evaluator error rates, especially for complex cross-app workflows with side-effects.

The evaluated shortcut generation methods are fairly basic (primarily prompt-based macro extraction from single trajectories), leaving more advanced code-synthesis, state-abstraction, and verification algorithms for agentic shortcut creation largely unaddressed.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: transitioning mobile GUI agents from pure step-by-step visual navigation to hybrid GUI-shortcut execution (leveraging APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts) to improve efficiency and success rates.
The benchmark design covers both shortcut utilization and shortcut generation, evaluating whether agents can autonomously abstract reusable workflows from interaction histories.

Comprehensive experimental setup across single-app and cross-app tasks, multiple modalities (screenshot visual agents vs. view hierarchy / UI tree agents), and detailed metrics capturing task completion, step ratio (MSRS), token cost (MToC), and execution time (MET).

Provides insightful findings, such as demonstrating that shortcut augmentation provides disproportionately larger performance leaps for weaker base models (e.g., Gemini-2.0-Flash) on complex cross-app workflows, and offering a concrete categorization of failure modes.
weaknesses: Model diversity in the experiments is quite limited: evaluations are conducted almost exclusively using the Gemini family (Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.0-Flash). Including leading proprietary alternatives (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) or open-source multimodal agents (e.g., Qwen2-VL) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.
The benchmark scale is moderate (139 tasks across 11 applications), and the shortcut generation experiments are further restricted to a 50% subset evaluated solely on the T3A baseline.

Dynamic mobile benchmarks relying on live, third-party commercial applications (e.g., Amazon, Booking.com, YouTube) inherently suffer from maintenance and reproducibility challenges due to frequent UI updates, network variations, and anti-bot/account-state mechanisms. The paper provides limited discussion on how environment state resets, app version pinning, and long-term stability are guaranteed.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated focus: Moving beyond pure GUI navigation to a hybrid GUI-shortcut paradigm (incorporating APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts) addresses critical practical bottlenecks in agent efficiency, latency, and token cost.

Dual-faceted benchmarking: In addition to measuring execution performance with curated shortcuts, the benchmark uniquely formalizes an evaluation protocol for assessing an agent's ability to self-generate reusable shortcuts from interaction traces.

Comprehensive metric suite: The paper evaluates agents across task success (SR), step efficiency (MS, MSRS), runtime (MET), token costs (MToC), and operational distribution (GSAR, SSR), offering a multi-dimensional view of agent behavior.

Insightful empirical findings: Experiments show that hybrid execution benefits both visual and view-hierarchy agent architectures, with disproportionately large reliability gains on smaller/weaker base models (Gemini-2.0-Flash).
weaknesses: Benchmark scale: With 139 tasks across 11 applications, the dataset is relatively small compared to concurrent mobile agent benchmarks (e.g., LlamaTouch with 495 tasks, SPA-Bench with 340 tasks), which limits statistical coverage across long-tail mobile interactions.

Reproducibility and app environment drift: Because the platform is deployed on real-world dynamic Android applications (e.g., YouTube, Amazon, Booking.com), background changes in live services, UI updates, and anti-bot/login barriers pose challenges for long-term evaluation reproducibility.

Model diversity: The empirical evaluation is restricted to the Gemini family (Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.0-Flash). Including open-weight agent models (e.g., Qwen2-VL or specialized GUI agents like SeeClick/UI-TARS) would strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

Underspecified shortcut retrieval: Section 4 mentions that relevant shortcuts are retrieved from the knowledge base and injected into the prompt context, but the paper lacks technical details regarding the retrieval mechanism (e.g., dense retriever architecture, top-$k$ selection, or whether all shortcuts are passed in-context).
